title: The Big Pumpkin Patch
sum: Rosie picks a pumpkin she can carry, saves its seeds all winter, and grows a pumpkin of her very own.

cast.d: a six-year-old girl who lives next door to her grandpa and wants the biggest pumpkin
cast.look: a six-year-old girl with curly brown hair, a green sweater and red rubber boots

cast.d: Rosie’s grandpa, who grows pumpkins in a patch behind his barn
cast.look: an older man with a short gray beard, a straw hat and blue overalls

cast.d: Grandpa’s dog, who sniffs and snacks on everything
cast.look: a floppy-eared brown dog with a white spot on his chest

p: Grandpa Ben had a pumpkin patch behind his barn. On Saturday, Rosie ran there in her red boots. Biscuit the dog ran even faster.
Grandpa came last, pulling the wagon. Squeak, squeak went the wheels. “Pick any pumpkin you like,” he said.
Rosie already knew which one. “The biggest,” she said. “The biggest one in the whole patch.”
Long vines crawled over the dirt like green ropes. The leaves were as big as dinner plates. Rosie touched one. It felt scratchy, like Grandpa’s chin.
Thin green curls grew out of the vines. They twisted around sticks and grass, like a pig’s tail. “Those help the vine hold on,” said Grandpa.
The first pumpkins were tiny and orange. They were as small as apples. Rosie picked one up with one hand. “Too small,” she said.
The next one was as big as a ball. But it was green all over. “Not that one,” said Grandpa. “Green means it’s not ready. Orange means it’s ready to pick.”
Rosie patted the green pumpkin. “See you in a few weeks,” she told it.
Then Biscuit barked. Woof! Woof! He was at the end of the row, sniffing something huge.
It was the biggest pumpkin Rosie had ever seen. It was even bigger than Biscuit. It was orange all over, with a thick, twisty stem.
“That one!” Rosie shouted. She grabbed it with both hands and pulled. The pumpkin did not move.
She pushed with her hands. She pushed with her shoulder. She pushed with her whole body. Nothing.
Rosie sat down in the dirt. Plop. Her cheeks were hot, and her arms felt like noodles. Biscuit licked her ear.
Grandpa knelt down next to her. “That pumpkin weighs more than you do,” he said. “Want to know my trick?”
He wrapped his arms around a pumpkin. “Give it a hug. If your hands meet, you can carry it.”
Rosie hugged the first pumpkin she saw. Too fat! Her fingers did not even touch.
She hugged the second one. Still too fat.
She hugged the third one. Squish! It had a soft brown spot. “Yuck!”
Then she hugged the fourth pumpkin. Her fingers met in the front, just barely. It was round and orange, with a short, dry stem.
Up it came! Rosie wobbled over, one step, two steps, three. Thump! The pumpkin landed in the wagon.
On the way back to the house, Rosie knocked on her pumpkin. Thunk, thunk. It sounded like a drum.
“What’s inside?” she asked. “Seeds,” said Grandpa. “Enough seeds for a whole pumpkin patch.”
Rosie’s eyes went wide. “A patch of my own?” She hugged her pumpkin tight. “Then I’ll grow the biggest one of all.”

art.s: A girl in red boots pulls with all her might on a giant orange pumpkin in a leafy pumpkin patch while a brown dog watches and an old man waits with a red wagon.

q.q: Which pumpkins were not ready to pick yet?
q.e: Green means not ready yet. Orange means ready to pick.

q.q: Draw Rosie’s face when the giant pumpkin would not move.
q.e: You can see just how Rosie felt!

q.q: Rosie tried Grandpa’s hug trick. How many pumpkins did she hug?
q.e: Too fat, still too fat, squishy, then just right. Four hugs!

p: That afternoon, Rosie’s pumpkin sat on Grandpa’s kitchen table. Grandpa cut a circle around the stem with his big knife. Then he lifted the top off, like a hat.
Rosie peeked inside. It was full of orange strings and flat white seeds. It smelled fresh, like a cucumber.
“Your turn,” said Grandpa. “Reach in and scoop it all out.” Rosie looked at the goop. She put her hands behind her back.
“It looks slimy,” she said. “It is slimy,” said Grandpa. He did not look sorry at all.
Rosie tried a spoon first. The seeds slid right off. Next she tried a soup ladle. The strings hung over the sides like wet spaghetti.
Under the table, Biscuit watched every drip. His tail went thump, thump on the floor.
Rosie took a big breath. She pushed one hand into the pumpkin. Squish! It was cold and wet and stringy.
“Eww!” she said. Then she wiggled her fingers. “Eww, eww, eww!” Now she was laughing.
Scoop, scoop, splat. Handfuls of goop landed in the bowl. Seeds stuck to her wrists. One even stuck to her nose.
Soon the pumpkin was empty inside. Rosie picked one seed out of the bowl. It was flat and white, shaped like a tiny teardrop.
“Is there a pumpkin in here?” she asked. “A baby plant is folded up inside,” said Grandpa. “Give it dirt, sun and water, and it can grow a whole new vine.”
Rosie looked at the bowl. There were so many seeds! “One, two, three…” At twenty, she lost her place.
“You don’t need them all,” said Grandpa. “Pick the ten fattest ones. Fat seeds grow best.”
Rosie picked out the fattest seeds and rinsed them in a cup of water. She laid them on a paper towel in two rows of five.
She counted them out loud. One, two, three, four, five. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Perfect.
Then a pink tongue came up over the edge of the table. Slurp! “Biscuit, no!” Rosie shouted.
Too late. One seed was gone. Biscuit licked his lips and wagged his tail.
Grandpa laughed. “Biscuit likes pumpkins too.” Rosie did not laugh. There was a gap in her second row now.
She carried the paper towel to the sunny windowsill, high above Biscuit’s nose. The seeds could dry there all week.
Then Rosie took a black marker and drew a face on her pumpkin. Two triangle eyes. A circle nose. A big smile with three square teeth.
Grandpa cut out the shapes with his knife. That night, a candle glowed inside. The pumpkin grinned at Biscuit, and Biscuit barked at it. Woof!

art.s: At a kitchen table, a girl pushes one hand into a hollow pumpkin full of orange strings while seeds stick to her nose and a brown dog looks up hopefully.

q.q: Rosie picked ten seeds. Biscuit ate one. How many were left?
q.e: One less than ten is nine. Nine seeds were left.

q.q: Grandpa said something is folded up inside each seed. What is it?
q.e: A tiny plant waits inside. Dirt, sun and water help it grow.

q.q: Draw Rosie’s hand in the pumpkin goop. Give her a speech bubble.
look: a hand in orange, stringy goop
q.e: Eww! That goop looks so slimy. Great speech bubble!

p: All week, Rosie’s seeds dried on Grandpa’s sunny windowsill. On Monday they were wet and slippery. By Friday they were dry and smooth, like little buttons.
On Saturday, the kitchen smelled warm and salty. Grandpa was roasting the rest of the pumpkin seeds. The tray sizzled when he pulled it out of the oven.
“Try one,” he said. Rosie bit a roasted seed. Crunch! It tasted salty, like a pretzel.
Then Grandpa reached for the windowsill. “A few more for the tray,” he said. He picked up Rosie’s paper towel.
“Stop!” Rosie shouted. “Those are my seeds!” Grandpa froze with the paper towel in the air.
Rosie took it with both hands and counted. All nine seeds were still there. “Phew,” she said.
Grandpa scratched his beard. “Sorry,” he said. “They all look the same to me.”
Rosie picked up each dry seed. Most were fat and smooth. But two of them were thin and flat.
She pinched a flat one. It bent like paper. Then she pinched a fat one. It was hard, like a tiny pebble.
Rosie held them both up to the window. The sun shone right through the flat seed. The fat seed stayed dark.
“The flat ones are empty,” said Grandpa. “No baby plant inside. Only the fat ones will grow.”
Rosie put the two flat seeds on the roasting tray. “You can have those,” she told Grandpa.
Grandpa gave her a small white envelope. Rosie dropped in the fat seeds, one at a time. Tap, tap, tap. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
She licked the flap and pressed it shut. Blech! It tasted like glue. Biscuit sniffed the envelope anyway.
Now the envelope needed a name. Rosie took a red marker. She wrote ROSIE’S SEEDS in big, wobbly letters.
Then she looked at Grandpa. He was crunching seeds. She looked at Biscuit. He was licking his lips.
Rosie added three more words. DO NOT EAT! She drew two lines under them.
Grandpa read the envelope out loud. “Rosie’s seeds. Do not eat.” He put his hand on his heart. “I promise.”
“Where do seeds sleep all winter?” Rosie asked. “Somewhere cool, dark and dry,” said Grandpa. “If they get warm and wet, they start to grow too soon.”
They put the envelope in an old tin box. Grandpa set the box on the highest shelf in the kitchen. Rosie stood on her tiptoes. She could just see the lid.
“How many sleeps until spring?” she asked. “Lots,” said Grandpa. He held out the bowl of roasted seeds.
Rosie took a big handful. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

art.s: A girl at a kitchen table writes big red letters on a small white envelope next to a tray of roasted pumpkin seeds, while a brown dog licks his lips.

q.q: How many fat seeds did Rosie put in the envelope?
q.e: Nine seeds, and two were flat. Seven fat seeds went in.

q.q: Rosie bit a roasted seed. What sound did it make?
q.e: Crunch! Roasted seeds are crunchy and salty.

q.q: Draw a fat seed and a flat seed. Circle the one that can grow.
look: a circle around the fat seed
q.e: You looked closely, just like Rosie. Only a fat seed has a baby plant inside.

p: All winter, the tin box sat on the high shelf. Then spring came. Snow slid off the barn roof, and the yard turned muddy and green.
Rosie climbed on a chair and got the box down. The envelope still said DO NOT EAT! She shook it. Rattle, rattle.
In the shed, Grandpa set out six yogurt cups and a bag of dirt. Rosie filled each cup to the top. The dirt was cool and smelled like rain.
She poked a hole in each cup with her finger. One seed went into each hole. But when she was done, one seed was left over.
“Seven seeds and six cups,” said Grandpa. “Keep that one for next year.” Rosie put it back in the envelope.
Biscuit’s tail thumped against the table. Thump, thump. The cups wobbled. Grandpa moved one cup to a shelf, next to the watering can.
Then he watered all six until the dirt turned dark. Rosie loaded the cups into her wagon and pulled them to the house.
She lined them up on the kitchen windowsill. The sun came in there all morning. Nobody looked at the shelf in the shed.
Every morning before school, Rosie ran next door to Grandpa’s kitchen. She gave each cup a little drink of water.
Then she sang to them. “Sun up high and water below. Little seeds, it’s time to grow!”
For four days, nothing happened. Rosie put her ear next to a cup. She could not hear a thing.
On the fifth day, a green hook poked out of the dirt. It looked like a tiny elbow. The next morning, it stood up straight and opened two smooth leaves.
Soon every cup on the windowsill had a sprout. Rosie counted them. One, two, three, four, five.
Then she counted on her fingers. Six seeds. Six cups. So where was number six?
Rosie looked under the table. She looked behind the curtain. She looked in Biscuit’s bed. Only an old sock.
The shed! Rosie ran across the wet grass in her socks. There on the shelf, next to the watering can, sat the sixth cup.
A sprout had come up in it, too. But it was tall, skinny and pale yellow. It flopped over the side of the cup like a wet noodle.
“It’s sick!” said Rosie. Grandpa peered around the dark shed.
“Not sick,” he said. “Just hungry for sun. Plants need light to turn green and strong.”
Rosie carried the cup back with both hands. Her wet socks went squish, squish on the kitchen floor. She set the cup in the sunniest spot, right in the middle.
Two days later, the pale sprout had turned green. It stood up straighter, too. Rosie named it Lucky.
Now six green sprouts stood in a row. Rosie sang her song six times, once for each cup. Biscuit sighed and went to sleep in the hall.

art.s: Inside a dim garden shed, a girl in wet socks finds a tall, pale yellow sprout flopping out of a yogurt cup on a shelf beside a watering can.

q.q: In Rosie’s song, which word rhymes with grow?
q.e: Below and grow end with the same sound. They rhyme!

q.q: Why was the sprout in the shed pale and yellow?
q.e: The shed was dark, so the sprout got no sun. By the window, it turned green.

q.q: Draw Rosie’s six cups in a row, with a sprout in each one.
q.e: Six cups, six sprouts. Lucky is one of them!

p: By June, the six sprouts were too big for their cups. Rosie and Grandpa planted them in a sunny corner of the patch. Rosie planted Lucky herself, right in the middle.
The sun shone and the rain came. The little plants grew into long vines. Lucky’s vine crawled out across the dirt, longer every week.
One day, Rosie measured the vines with her feet. Heel, toe, heel, toe. Lucky’s vine was ten steps long. The others were only seven.
Then big yellow flowers opened along the vines. They were shaped like trumpets. Rosie counted eight flowers on Lucky alone.
Bees zoomed in and out of the flowers. Bzzz. Their fuzzy legs were covered in yellow dust. The bees did not care about Rosie one bit.
Biscuit snapped at one bee. It buzzed right past his nose, and he backed away fast. “Leave them alone,” said Grandpa. “They’re working.”
“Working?” asked Rosie. “They carry that yellow dust from flower to flower,” said Grandpa. “That’s how a pumpkin gets started.”
The next morning, Rosie ran out to see Lucky. Oh no! The flowers had closed up tight. Two lay on the ground, brown and floppy.
“Lucky is broken!” said Rosie. Her chin started to wobble.
Grandpa knelt down and lifted a big leaf. Under one closed flower was a little green ball, as small as a marble. “Look,” he said. “A baby pumpkin.”
Rosie looked under every leaf on Lucky. One green marble. Two green marbles. Three!
Every hot afternoon, Rosie gave Lucky a big drink from the hose. Glug, glug, glug. The three green balls grew as big as oranges. Then they grew as big as soccer balls.
By October, the leaves were dry and crunchy under Rosie’s boots. The three pumpkins had turned from green to orange.
Rosie looked at them. One was big, one was middle-sized, and one was small. The big one was not the biggest in the patch. But it was hers.
Rosie hugged the big one. Her fingers met in the front, just barely. She lifted. Up it came!
She carried it to the wagon all by herself. Thump! Biscuit sniffed it all over and wagged his tail.
“So how do you grow a pumpkin?” asked Grandpa. Rosie counted on her fingers.
“First a seed,” she said. “Then a sprout. Next, a vine with yellow flowers. Last, a pumpkin!”
Grandpa knocked on her pumpkin. Thunk, thunk. “What’s inside?” he asked.
Rosie grinned. “Seeds,” she said. “Enough for a whole patch.”

art.s: In a sunny pumpkin patch, a girl hugs an orange pumpkin beside a long vine with yellow trumpet flowers and buzzing bees, while a brown dog sniffs a red wagon.

q.q: Rosie told the steps in order. What came right after the sprout?
q.e: First a seed, then a sprout, next a vine. Last, a pumpkin!

q.q: How many baby pumpkins did Rosie find under the flowers?
q.e: One, two, three green marbles. They grew into three pumpkins.

q.q: Draw a bee on a yellow pumpkin flower. Show the yellow dust.
q.e: Bzzz! Your bee is helping a pumpkin get started.

fin.q: Rosie grew pumpkins from seeds. Where did she get those seeds?
fin.e: She scooped them out of the pumpkin she picked, then saved them all winter.

fin.q: Which of these did Rosie do first?
c: Found a cup in the shed
fin.e: First she scooped the seeds. Later came the cups, the shed and the bees.
